# Problem 6: Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

200 students surveyed, 128 reported being satisfied with the online learning resources.

**(a) Sample proportion.**

```{r p6-a}
x = 128
n = 200
p_hat = x/n
cat("Sample proportion:", p_hat, "\n")
```

**(b) 95% confidence interval.** We use `prop.test()`.

```{r p6-b}
ci_test = prop.test(x, n, conf.level = 0.95)
ci_test
```

**(c) Endpoints and interpretation.**

```{r p6-c}
ci = ci_test$conf.int
cat("Lower endpoint:", ci[1], "\n")
cat("Upper endpoint:", ci[2], "\n")
```

We are 95% confident that the true proportion of students who are satisfied with the online learning resources is between `r round(ci[1], 4)` and `r round(ci[2], 4)`.

**(d) Comparison with Problem 1.** The Problem 1 interval is the Wald interval.

```{r p6-d}
wald = p_hat + c(-1, 1)*1.96*sqrt(p_hat*(1 - p_hat)/n)
cat("Wald interval (Problem 1):", wald, "\n")
cat("prop.test() interval:     ", ci, "\n")
```

The endpoints differ for two reasons. First, `prop.test()` reports a Wilson score interval, not a Wald interval. Second, `prop.test()` uses a continuity correction, which makes the interval slightly wider. Both intervals give about the same result.

# Problem 7: Hypothesis Test for a Population Proportion

Of the 200 students surveyed, 142 support the policy. We test $H_0: p = 0.60$ versus $H_a: p \ne 0.60$ at $\alpha = 0.05$.

**(a) Two-sided test.** We use `correct = FALSE` and set the null value with `p`.

```{r p7-a}
x = 142
n = 200
p0 = 0.60

test = prop.test(x, n, p = p0, alternative = "two.sided", correct = FALSE)
test
```

**(b) Test statistic.** We check that the X-squared statistic equals $z^2$ from Problem 2.

```{r p7-b}
p_hat = x/n
z = (p_hat - p0)/sqrt(p0*(1 - p0)/n)

cat("X-squared:", test$statistic, "\n")
cat("Degrees of freedom:", test$parameter, "\n")
cat("p-value:", test$p.value, "\n")
cat("z:", z, "\n")
cat("z squared:", z^2, "\n")
```

The X-squared statistic is `r round(test$statistic, 3)`, which equals $z^2$ = `r round(z^2, 3)`.

**(c) Confidence interval.** We compare the interval from R with the Wald interval.

```{r p7-c}
ci = test$conf.int
wald = p_hat + c(-1, 1)*1.96*sqrt(p_hat*(1 - p_hat)/n)

cat("prop.test() interval (Wilson):", ci, "\n")
cat("Wald interval:               ", wald, "\n")
```

The endpoints differ slightly because `prop.test()` reports a Wilson score interval even when `correct = FALSE`. The Wilson interval is not centered at $\hat{p}$, while the Wald interval is.

**(d) Interval and test.** The null value 0.60 is not inside the 95% confidence interval, which matches rejecting $H_0$ at the 5% level.

**(e) Conclusion.** The p-value (`r signif(test$p.value, 3)`) is less than 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. There is sufficient evidence that the proportion of students who support the policy differs from 60%. The sample proportion is `r p_hat`, so support appears to be higher than claimed.

# Problem 8: Chi-Squared Goodness-of-Fit Test in R

$H_0$: the distribution of study locations matches the claimed distribution. $H_a$: at least one proportion is different.

**(a) Observed counts.**

```{r p8-a}
observed = c(86, 54, 38, 22)
names(observed) = c("Library", "Residence hall", "Student center", "Other")
observed
```

**(b) Expected proportions.**

```{r p8-b}
claimed = c(0.40, 0.30, 0.20, 0.10)
claimed
```

**(c) Goodness-of-fit test.**

```{r p8-c}
gof = chisq.test(observed, p = claimed)
gof
gof$expected
```

**(d) Test statistic, degrees of freedom, and p-value.**

```{r p8-d}
cat("X-squared:", gof$statistic, "\n")
cat("Degrees of freedom:", gof$parameter, "\n")
cat("p-value:", gof$p.value, "\n")
```

**(e) Comparison and conclusion.** We check the result against the hand calculation from Problem 4.

```{r p8-e}
E = 200*claimed
chi_hand = sum((observed - E)^2/E)
cat("Chi-squared by hand:", chi_hand, "\n")
```

The hand calculation matches R. The p-value (`r round(gof$p.value, 3)`) is greater than 0.05, so we fail to reject $H_0$. There is not sufficient evidence that the distribution of preferred study locations differs from the claimed distribution.

# Problem 9: Chi-Squared Test of Independence in R

$H_0$: class format and exam outcome are independent. $H_a$: they are associated.

**(a) Observed counts.**

```{r p9-a}
tab = matrix(c(66, 64, 34, 76), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(tab) = c("In-person", "Online")
colnames(tab) = c("Passed", "Failed")
tab
```

**(b) Test without continuity correction.**

```{r p9-b}
test = chisq.test(tab, correct = FALSE)
test
```

**(c) Test statistic, degrees of freedom, and p-value.**

```{r p9-c}
cat("X-squared:", test$statistic, "\n")
cat("Degrees of freedom:", test$parameter, "\n")
cat("p-value:", test$p.value, "\n")
```

**(d) Expected counts and Yates' correction.** The expected counts from R match Problem 5.

```{r p9-d}
test$expected

E_hand = outer(rowSums(tab), colSums(tab))/sum(tab)
E_hand

test_yates = chisq.test(tab)
test_yates
```

By default, R applies Yates' continuity correction to 2 x 2 tables. It subtracts 0.5 from each $|O - E|$ before squaring, so the test statistic gets smaller (`r round(test$statistic, 3)` to `r round(test_yates$statistic, 3)`) and the p-value gets larger (`r round(test$p.value, 4)` to `r round(test_yates$p.value, 4)`).

**(e) Conclusion.** The p-value (`r round(test$p.value, 4)`) is less than 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. There is sufficient evidence of an association between class format and exam outcome. In the sample, `r round(100*66/130, 1)`% of in-person students passed compared with `r round(100*34/110, 1)`% of online students. This does not show that class format causes the difference, because students were not randomly assigned and other factors could explain it.
